issues.issue: The execution date is left blank ("made as of June __, 2004"), so the date on which this Agreement took effect cannot be determined from its own words. A court would have to construe when, or whether, the instrument became operative as between LSB and DMSA.

"Control" is defined only as the "power to direct or cause the direction of the management and policies of a Person," with no ownership threshold or other boundary. Whether a given DMSA entity is an "Affiliate" for purposes of Section 12.7's outside-business licence therefore has no determinate answer.

Capital Contribution is measured by "the fair market value of any property (other than money) contributed," but neither this definition nor Schedule A states who values non-cash contributions or when. DMSA's initial capital under the Venture Agreement was to include travel, legal fees and staff labor, so the valuation gap has real work to do.

"Covered Person" sweeps in every Affiliate, officer, employee, representative or agent of a Member, which makes the indemnity in Section 12.4 run to persons who are strangers to the Agreement. Its outer boundary ("representatives") is undefined.

Clause (iii) refers to "the period described in Clause (ii) of this sentence," but the clauses are mis-numbered in the text ((i), (11), (iii)), so which period is cross-referenced is uncertain. The mechanical numbering error changes what a partial Fiscal Year is.

The definition of "Interest" is internally garbled — "such Member's interest of the profits and losses" — and bundles voting, profit and distribution rights without saying whether a transfer of one carries the others. Article XVI's transfer machinery turns on exactly that.

The enumeration of "Laws" ends with the open-ended category "all policies, practices and guidelines of any governmental body," which is far broader than the binding instruments listed before it. Whether non-binding agency guidance counts as "Law" for provisions such as Section 9.3 is left unresolved.

"Majority" is defined as a quantity of Member Votes, yet Section 5.5(vii) speaks of "A Majority present in person or by proxy" as if it were a person. The definition cannot be substituted into the operative text without incoherence.

"Members" is defined as "two (2) or more of such Persons," so provisions conditioned on action by "the Members" (e.g. Sections 2.4 and 8.2(i)) arguably require both LSB and DMSA acting together rather than a Majority Vote. With only two members the plural definition and the voting provisions pull apart.

Member Votes are whatever Schedule A "as may be amended" says, but this definition names no procedure or consent requirement for amending Schedule A, while Section 17.10 requires unanimity for amendments and Section 2.1(iii) lets the Secretary update Schedule A unilaterally. How voting power can lawfully be changed is therefore in doubt.

Net Cash Flow is reduced by "any amounts determined by the Members to be necessary to provide a reasonable reserve," yet Section 9.2 commits the timing and amount of all distributions to the Board. Whether Members or the Board set reserves cannot be squared from the two provisions.

Percentage Interest is fixed "as shown on Schedule A" but simultaneously "as determined by the unanimous written consent of the Members as adjusted from time to time," which does not square with Section 2.1(iii) authorising the Secretary to update Schedule A without member consent. Which mechanism governs an adjustment of ownership is unresolved.

The list of entities in "Person" uses the defined term "Company," which Article I fixes as Dialogo, LLC itself, evidently in place of "corporation." Read literally, the definition of Person excludes corporations generally.

Profits and Losses are defined purely as taxable income or loss under § 703(a), with none of the book adjustments that Section 4.4(ii) and Section 8.2(iv) presuppose by requiring Capital Accounts and allocations to comply with Treasury Regulation § 1.704-1(b) and Code § 704(b). The tax definition and the 704(b) capital-account regime cannot both be applied as written.

Membership is made to turn on "execution of this Agreement or a counterpart," but the instrument as filed bears a blank date and no executed signature page. Whether LSB and DMSA ever became Members under this provision is a live question.

This provision says a revision to Schedule A "shall not be deemed an amendment to this Agreement," while Schedule A fixes Percentage Interests, Member Votes and Capital Contributions that Section 17.10 makes amendable only by unanimous written vote of all Members. The two provisions cannot both be given effect if the Secretary revises Schedule A alone.

The provision obliges "Gerry Pike," a person who is not a party to the Agreement and holds no office defined in it, to execute and file the Articles. Whose obligation this is if Pike does not act is unstated.

The power to designate a new registered agent or office is given to "the Members," whereas Section 2.6 gives the Board the corresponding qualification and filing functions and Section 5.1 leaves the Members no power to bind the Company individually. Who may change the agent, and by what vote, is not squared.

The Secretary is directed to file qualification certificates for any jurisdiction "in which the Company may wish to conduct business," while the preceding sentence ties the duty to jurisdictions where it "transacts business." The two standards fix different triggers within the same section.

The stated object — "developing Spanish language newspaper(s) and media" — is immediately swallowed by the general "any lawful act or activity for which limited liability companies may be formed," so the specific purpose sets no boundary on the Company's field. That boundary matters because Section 12.7 makes LSB's exclusivity run to "the business" and DMSA free to compete outside it.

Merger requires "approval of all of the Members," but Section 6.8 vests decisions on dispositions of assets and equity issuances in a unanimous Board and Section 6.1 gives the Board management of the business generally. Whether a merger also needs Board action is left open.

The recitation that each Member "has contributed or is deemed to have contributed" the Schedule A amount cannot be squared with Schedule A itself, which lists LSB at the garbled figure "$00,001.00," and with the Venture Agreement's acknowledgement that LSB would contribute no cash. What LSB in fact contributed for her 49% is unresolved.

No Member may be required to make additional capital contributions, which does not square with the Venture Agreement's provision that DMSA "shall contribute the initial capital to launch the LLC" in an amount DMSA deems appropriate. Whether DMSA's funding commitment survives this Agreement is a question of which instrument governs.

Returns of Capital Contributions must be made "to all Members in proportion to their Percentage Interests," which cannot be squared with Section 6.8(iii) permitting distributions only "to reimburse DMSA for initial capital contributions." A repayment of DMSA's launch capital is either a pro-rata return or a DMSA-only reimbursement, not both.

Exception (a) — "the respective invoices of each of DMSA" — is grammatically incomplete, so it cannot be told whether the payment right belongs to DMSA alone or to each of DMSA and LSB. Exception (b) then pays profits per "Membership Interests," a term the Agreement never defines.

The bar on any Member receiving salary or compensation for services conflicts with Section 12.7's requirement that LSB "employ its diligent efforts for the Company" exclusively, and with the Venture Agreement's designation of LSB as Publisher running day-to-day operations. Whether LSB could be paid for full-time service is exactly what these provisions leave unsettled.

The phrase "the Members shall be able only to make their capital contributions pursuant to Section 4.1" is garbled — "be able only" reads as a prohibition where an obligation limit was intended. Whether it forbids further contributions that Section 4.1(ii) expressly permits by unanimous consent is the resulting question.

Capital Accounts must be maintained under Treasury Regulation § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iv), a book-value regime, while Article I defines Profits and Losses as bare § 703(a) taxable income and Section 10.2 fixes the accrual method for determining them. The account balances that Section 15.3 liquidates on cannot be computed consistently under both.

A Member advance is made "subject to such terms and conditions acceptable to the Company and each Member," which supplies no rate, maturity or default mechanism and requires an agreement that may never be reached. Whether an advance made without such agreement is a debt at all is left open.

Section 5.1 gives the Members "any and all other rights or powers of the Company" not required to be exercised by the Board, while Section 6.1 vests management of the business and affairs in the Board "[s]ubject to Section 5.1." The two provisions are mutually deferential and leave the Member/Board boundary circular.

Mandatory reimbursement of "all ordinary and necessary out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Members on behalf of the Company" does not square with the Venture Agreement's rule that no member may incur costs on the LLC's behalf except in accordance with the approved budget, nor with Section 6.8(ix)'s unanimous-Board budget requirement. Whether unbudgeted expenses must be reimbursed is the contest.

The flat bar on resignation cannot be squared with Section 15.2(ii), which treats "the resignation ... of a Member" as an event dissolving the Company unless the remaining Members agree to continue. One provision forbids what the other assumes can happen.

The annual meeting is to be held "in each year" at a place designated by the Board, but no date, month or default calling mechanism is fixed, and the special-meeting sentence omits who fixes the time and place. If no annual meeting is called, the election machinery in Sections 5.5(ii) and 6.1 has no trigger.

Director elections are allotted one to LSB and two to DMSA, which cannot be squared with Section 5.5(viii)'s rule that a Majority Vote decides "any question brought before such meeting" and with Section 6.1's statement that Directors are elected at the annual meeting of the Members. Whether board seats are elected by class or by Member Vote is left in doubt.

Special meetings may be called only by the President or, on written request of a Board majority, by the President or Secretary, so a Member holding a Majority has no way to convene the Members. That leaves Section 5.5(viii)'s Majority Vote power with no self-executing route to a meeting.

Quorum is "[a] Majority present in person or by proxy," which under the Article I definition means DMSA's 51 votes alone, so DMSA can constitute a meeting and transact business without LSB. That sits against the provisions requiring the consent of "all of the Members" (e.g. Sections 4.1(ii), 13.1 and 17.10).

Action without a meeting may be taken on the signature of "a Majority" — DMSA alone — even though Section 17.10 and Sections 4.1(ii), 13.1 and 15.2(i) require the assent of all Members for particular acts. The "[u]nless otherwise provided" opener does not say whether those unanimity provisions are among the exceptions.

Management is vested in the Board "[s]ubject to Section 5.1," and Section 5.1 in turn reserves to the Members every power not required to be exercised by the Board — a circular allocation of authority. Which body may act on a matter neither provision names is unresolvable from the text.

The quorum rule is made subject to "Section 6.9 of this Agreement," but there is no Section 6.9; the unanimous-approval provision is Section 6.8. The exception to majority Board action therefore points at nothing.

A committee may consist of "one or more of the Directors," so a single director — necessarily a DMSA or LSB appointee — could exercise Board powers under Section 6.5's third paragraph. That sits uneasily with Section 6.3's majority quorum requirement for Board action.

The carve-out from committee authority is defined by reference to "the actions described in Section 6.9 of this Agreement," and no Section 6.9 exists — the unanimous-approval list is Section 6.8. The limit on delegated committee power thus has no identified content.

This compensation provision is numbered "Section 6.6," the same number carried by the Removal of Directors section that follows it, and it is run into the end of Section 6.5 without a break. The duplicate numbering makes cross-references to "Section 6.6" ambiguous.

This removal provision is also numbered "Section 6.6," duplicating the Compensation of Directors section immediately above it, so any reference to Section 6.6 is ambiguous. The mis-numbering also leaves the Article's sequence (6.5, 6.6, 6.6, 6.7, 6.8) out of step with the cross-references to "Section 6.9" elsewhere.

Clause (iii) bars "the declaration or making of any distributions to Members other than to reimburse DMSA for initial capital contributions," which cannot be squared with Section 9.1's requirement that Net Cash Flow be distributed in proportion to Percentage Interests, or with the Venture Agreement's mandatory annual tax distributions. Whether LSB can ever receive a distribution turns on which provision controls.

The unanimity triggers in clauses (viii) and (xiv) turn on whether a capital expenditure or liability is "material," a term the Agreement nowhere defines or quantifies. Whether a given commitment needed unanimous Board approval is therefore indeterminate.

Officers are elected and removable by "the affirmative vote of a majority of the Board," which on a board of one LSB appointee and two DMSA appointees lets DMSA install and remove the President and Secretary at will, notwithstanding the Venture Agreement's designation of LSB as Publisher with day-to-day management. The provision's interaction with Section 5.5(ii)'s allocation of board seats is where the fight lies.

The President is given "general and active management of the business of the Company," which overlaps the Board's management of "the business and affairs" under Section 6.1 and the unanimous-Board list in Section 6.8. Where presidential management ends and Board authorisation begins is not drawn.

The Secretary is placed "under whose supervision" of both "the Board or President," while Section 2.1(iii) obliges the Secretary to update Schedule A and Section 2.6 to make qualification filings on her own authority. Whether the Secretary's Schedule A and filing duties are subject to Board or presidential direction is unsettled.

This section imposes on each Director the corporate fiduciary duties of loyalty and care, which cannot be squared with Section 12.7 expressly relieving DMSA "of its fiduciary duties as a Director" to pursue competing ventures, or with Section 12.3's replacement of duties existing at law. Whether a DMSA-affiliated director owes a duty of loyalty is precisely the collision.

Losses are allocated strictly in proportion to Percentage Interests with no deficit-restoration or qualified-income-offset provision, even though Section 8.2(iv) declares the allocations intended to comply with Code § 704(b). Whether losses can be allocated 49% to LSB, who made little or no capital contribution, is the question.

The residual allocation is made "in the same proportions as they shared Interest Profits and Losses," a garbled phrase — "Interest Profits" is not a defined or usable term anywhere in the Agreement. What proportion governs the catch-all allocation is therefore unclear.

Distribution of Net Cash Flow in proportion to Percentage Interests cannot be squared with Section 6.8(iii), which forbids any distribution to Members except reimbursement of DMSA's initial capital contributions. The Venture Agreement's waterfall repaying DMSA's launch capital first compounds the conflict.

Committing all distributions to the Board's unfettered timing and amount does not square with the Venture Agreement's undertaking that the board "shall distribute each year at least enough cash to owners to cover the owners' U.S. tax liability." Whether the minimum tax distribution survives is the question.

The books must be kept with "a copy of this Agreement and of the Certificate," but "Certificate" is not a defined term — Article I defines "Articles" for the organizational document. What document must be kept available for member inspection is left to construction.

The books must be kept on "the accrual method of accounting" for determining Profits and Losses, while the Article I definition of Net Cash Flow requires that it "be determined in accordance with the cash receipts and disbursements method of accounting." The two accounting mandates cannot both govern the Company's records.

Exculpation turns on acts performed "in good faith" and "in a manner reasonably believed to be within the scope of authority conferred," with liability preserved only for "gross negligence or willful misconduct" — none of which is defined. Whether DMSA's diversion of business to itself falls inside or outside the carve-out is the resulting question.

This clause begins mid-sentence ("professional or expert competence and who has been selected with reasonable care...") with its subject and operative verb missing from the instrument. What protection Section 12.2(ii) confers, and on whom, cannot be read off the text.

Section 12.3 declares that the Agreement's provisions "replace" a Covered Person's duties otherwise existing at law or in equity, which cannot be squared with Section 7.7's imposition on each Director and Officer of the fiduciary duties of loyalty and care under the Maine Business Corporation Act. Whether common-law fiduciary duty survives is the collision.

Indemnification runs "[t]o the fullest extent permitted by applicable law" to every Covered Person, a class defined to include Members' affiliates, employees and agents, while Section 17.11 confers rights under the Agreement on no Person "except the Members and Managers." Who may actually enforce the indemnity is unresolved.

The section breaks off mid-sentence at "against any liability that may be asserted," so the scope of the insurance the Company may buy — and whether it extends to liabilities not indemnifiable under Section 12.4 — is missing from the text. The provision cannot be applied as written.

LSB's exclusivity — she "shall not provide such services, directly or indirectly for itself or any other entity or person to the extent it relates to the business" — leaves "such services" and "the business" undefined, with no geographic or temporal limit. The first sentence is also garbled ("and the Company the income or profits derived therefrom"), so DMSA's licence to compete is stated in incomplete words.

The section expressly relieves DMSA "of its fiduciary duties as a Director" while Section 7.7 imposes the duties of loyalty and care of a corporate director on every Director, and DMSA is a Member rather than a Director at all. The two cannot both be given effect as to DMSA's board designees.

Disclosure is barred "without the prior written consent of the LLC," but "LLC" is not a defined term in this Agreement — Article I defines "Company" — and no organ is identified as able to give that consent. The obligation also has no time limit or carve-out for publicly known information.

"Proprietary Information" is defined by a closed list of categories (advertiser and subscription lists, marketing, product, strategic, financial, supplier information, billing rates) with no residual catch-all and no exclusion for information already public or independently known. The list also differs from the parallel definition in the Venture Agreement, which speaks of advertising and subscription client lists and client-provided information.

Admission of an Additional Member requires "approval of all of the Members," while Section 6.8(vii) forbids the issuance of any Interest without unanimous Board authorisation and the Venture Agreement requires Board approval for issuing additional membership interests. Whether member unanimity alone suffices cannot be answered from this section.

The prohibition is circular — assignment is barred "without complying with the terms of this Agreement" — and Article XIV states no procedure at all, the transfer machinery sitting in Article XVI. Which terms an assignor must comply with is left to be worked out elsewhere.

Only assignments or pledges "in violation of this Article XIV" are made invalid, yet the substantive transfer restrictions — right of first refusal, securities opinion, transferee undertaking — are in Article XVI. A transfer that breaches Article XVI is not caught by this invalidation clause.

A pledge requires "prior written consent of all Members," which cannot be squared with Section 16.8 empowering the Board alone to waive "any transfer restrictions contained in this Agreement," transfer being defined in Section 16.2 to include a transfer "as security." Whose consent a pledge needs is therefore contested.

Clause (ii) treats the "resignation" or "retirement" of a Member as a dissolution event, though Section 5.4 forbids a Member to resign before dissolution and winding up. The two provisions cannot both be given effect.

Liquidating proceeds are distributed "to the Members in accordance with their Capital Account balances," which does not square with Section 9.1's Percentage Interest distributions or with Section 6.8(iii) limiting distributions to reimbursement of DMSA's initial capital. On Schedule A's figures the two measures produce sharply different results for LSB.

Ownership is fixed by whose name "stand[s] on Schedule A," a schedule Section 2.1(iii) lets the Secretary update unilaterally and Section 2.1(iii) says is not an amendment to the Agreement. Record ownership of Interests can thus be changed without member action.

"Transfer" is defined to include involuntary transfers, testamentary transfers and transfers "by division of marital property," yet the only sanction stated is suspension of voting and distribution rights, and the section restricts transfers "except in compliance with the restrictions on transfer set forth below" — restrictions that include cross-references to non-existent Sections 16.9 to 16.11. What a transferee by operation of law actually receives is unresolved.

The section refers to transfers "pursuant to Sections 16.9, 16.10, and 16.11 of this Agreement," none of which exists, and the sentence itself breaks off after "the Company and the other Members shall." The waiver it purports to create has neither trigger nor content.

The securities-opinion requirement may be waived by the Board or the President "for good cause," a standard the Agreement nowhere defines, and the opinion must be "in form and substance Satisfactory" to them without limit. Whether a refusal to waive or to accept an opinion is reviewable is left open.

The notice must state "the Percentage Interests and number of LLC Votes to be transferred," but "LLC Votes" is not a defined term — Article I defines "Member Votes." The acceptance sentence also ends without stating any period within which the Company or Members must accept the deemed offer.

This part conditions the transferring Member's freedom to sell on acceptance and closing not occurring "within the periods set forth above," but the preceding part of Section 16.6 fixes no acceptance period at all. The right of first refusal has no ascertainable deadline.

The Board may waive "any transfer restrictions contained in this Agreement" "[n]otwithstanding anything to the contrary," which cannot be squared with Section 14.3's requirement of all Members' written consent to a pledge or with Section 13.1's requirement of unanimous member approval to admit a transferee as a Member. Board waiver would override protections the Members reserved to themselves.

Notices to the Company go to "the address specified in Section 2.5," which Section 2.5 lets the Board change at any time without any obligation to notify the Members. A Member could serve a valid notice at a superseded address, or fail to.

The Agreement is made binding on the parties' "successors, legal representatives and assigns" "to the extent permitted by this Agreement," while Sections 14.1, 16.2 and 16.3 make assignments invalid unless the transferee undertakes to become a party. Which assignees take the benefit of the Agreement is not settled by this section.

The integration clause declares this Agreement the entire agreement and superseding "all prior agreements and understandings pertaining thereto," which would displace the parties' earlier Venture Agreement on the same subject — LSB's exclusivity, DMSA's outside businesses, the distribution waterfall and tax distributions. Whether the Venture Agreement survives, and to what extent, is exactly what this clause puts in issue.

Amendments require the affirmative vote of all Members in a writing executed by all Members, which cannot be squared with Section 2.1(iii) permitting the Secretary to revise Schedule A — the source of Percentage Interests and Member Votes — without any amendment. The unanimity protection is only as strong as Schedule A's exemption from it.

Rights are confined to "the Members and Managers," yet Sections 12.4 and 12.5 confer indemnification and expense-advance rights on "Covered Persons," a class expressly including Officers, Affiliates, employees and agents who are neither Members nor Managers. Whether those persons can enforce the indemnity is left contradictory.
